idiom_name: struct command with function pointers + mutex/condvar ring buffer + pthread workers
implementation_notes: C ships no command type, no queue and no executor, so all three are built by hand: define a command as a struct whose first fields are the operations (`void (*execute)(struct command *)`, `void (*undo)(struct command *)`) plus a payload pointer, and let each constructor fill them in. Ready commands live in a bounded ring buffer protected by a pthread_mutex_t and a pthread_cond_t; worker threads block in pthread_cond_wait and pop one command at a time, executing it outside the lock. Where a queue already exists - POSIX message queues (mq_open/mq_send/mq_receive) or a GLib main loop with g_idle_add/source dispatch - it supplies transport and scheduling, but the command abstraction, the history list for undo and macro grouping remain yours to write. The classic hand-built structure is the norm in C because nothing replaces it.
pitfalls: Calling pthread_cond_wait without a `while` re-check (or signalling before waiting) loses wakeups, so queued commands sit unprocessed.
The payload pointer must be owned by exactly one party: commands that are pushed onto a history list after execution are a classic double-free or leak site when ownership is informal.
Executing a command while holding the queue mutex serialises every worker and deadlocks as soon as a command enqueues a follow-up command.
Function pointers carry no data, so a command that needs state must allocate it; unbounded allocation per request turns a load spike into fragmentation or OOM.
